---
title: "Simulation Study Theory"
---

## Introduction {#sec-sim-intro}

The theorems of Parts II to V are limit statements. They certify that an estimator is *consistent*: that
matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) recovers the target contrast as the index sample grows
(@thm-anchored-maic-consistency), that the unanchored estimators do so only under the far stronger
absolute-constancy hypothesis (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency), that multilevel network meta-regression
removes the aggregation bias a standard network meta-analysis cannot (@thm-aggregation-bias,
@thm-failure-of-bucher). What these theorems do not say is how an estimator behaves at the sample sizes a
health-technology-assessment dossier actually carries: a single index trial of a few hundred patients, a
comparator known only through a published mean. Consistency is a statement about the horizon; the analyst
stands at a finite distance from it. Four questions remain open at that distance, and none of them is
answerable by a limit theorem alone.

How large is the finite-sample bias, and is the residual bias of an "asymptotically unbiased" method
negligible at the sample size in hand? How does one method's variance compare with another's, so that a
slightly biased but stable estimator can be preferred to an unbiased but volatile one? Do the nominal
ninety-five percent confidence intervals actually contain the truth ninety-five percent of the time, or
does the variance approximation that produced them quietly fail? And how do all of these degrade when the
method's assumptions are violated, when an effect modifier is omitted, when the populations barely overlap,
when the outcome model is wrong? These are empirical questions about the *sampling distribution* of an
estimator at finite $n$, and the instrument that answers them is the **simulation study**: fix a
data-generating mechanism whose truth you control, draw many datasets from it, apply each candidate method
to each dataset, and summarize how the resulting estimates scatter around the known target. The decisive advantage of this
instrument is that in a simulation we build the world ourselves, so the truth is known by construction:
unlike a real analysis, where the target effect can never be observed and an estimator's error can only be
guessed at, a simulation lets us measure that error directly, by comparing every estimate against the number
we put in.

This chapter is the mathematics of that instrument. The central conceptual move, which organizes
everything that follows, is to recognize that a simulation study has *two* sample sizes, governing *two*
asymptotics. The first is $n$, the size of each simulated dataset; it controls the statistical behavior of
the estimator and is the variable in every consistency theorem of the preceding chapters. The second is
$R$, the number of simulated datasets, the *replications*; it controls how precisely the simulation
*measures* that behavior, and it is a budget the analyst sets, not a feature of the data. A performance
measure such as bias or coverage is a *functional* of the estimator's sampling distribution at a fixed $n$,
hence a fixed but unknown number; here a functional is simply a rule that takes an entire distribution as its
input and returns a single number, the way a mean or a variance summarizes a distribution, and the sampling
distribution in question, written $F_n$ and defined precisely in @def-sim-performance-functional below, is
what the average estimates; the simulation estimates it by a Monte Carlo average over the $R$
replications, an estimate that carries its own sampling error. Confusing the two asymptotics is the
cardinal sin of simulation practice: reporting a bias to four decimal places from $R=100$ replications, or
declaring two methods' coverages different when the difference is within Monte Carlo noise. We will be
scrupulous about keeping them apart, and the recurring discipline is to attach to every reported
performance number a **Monte Carlo standard error** (MCSE) that quantifies the $R$-driven uncertainty.

::: {.remark}
**A running clinical example.** To keep the symbols attached to something concrete, we illustrate every
performance measure on one indirect comparison, returned to at each step and worked in full in
@sec-sim-example. A health-technology-assessment team must compare a new interleukin-23 inhibitor $A$ against
an established interleukin-17 inhibitor $B$ for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. No head-to-head trial
exists; instead an index trial compares $A$ against ustekinumab $C$ with full individual patient data, while
a published trial compares $B$ against the same ustekinumab $C$ but reports only arm means. The common
comparator $C$ anchors the comparison (the *anchored* setting of Chapter 17). The endpoint is the reduction
in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score from baseline to week 16, measured in points, so the
natural scale is the identity (mean-difference) scale. Two baseline covariates matter: an effect modifier
$x_1$ (baseline disease severity, which changes how large the treatment benefit is) and a purely prognostic
covariate $x_2$ (age, which shifts outcomes but not the benefit). The target estimand is the marginal
$A$-versus-$B$ mean difference in the comparator trial's population, $\theta=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$. All
numbers used below are illustrative, chosen for arithmetic transparency, not taken from real trials.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The two sample sizes of a simulation, and the two limits they govern, can be laid side by side. The columns
are independent: a large $R$ cannot cure a small-$n$ deficiency, and a large $n$ cannot excuse too few
replications.

| | Within one replication | Across replications |
|---|---|---|
| Sample size | $n$: patients per simulated dataset | $R$: number of simulated datasets |
| Set by | the scenario, to mimic a real trial size | the analyst's computing budget |
| Governs | the estimator's true behavior (bias, variance, coverage at that $n$) | how precisely the simulation *measures* that behavior |
| Limit | statistical limit $n\to\infty$: the consistency theorems of Parts II to V | Monte Carlo limit $R\to\infty$: shrinks every MCSE at rate $1/\sqrt{R}$ |
| Error controlled | the method's finite-sample error | the simulation's own reporting error, the MCSE |

The plan is as follows. @sec-sim-ademp sets out the **ADEMP** framework of @morris2019ademp, the
now-standard checklist (aims, data-generating mechanism, estimands, methods, performance measures) that
disciplines the design and reporting of a simulation study, and formalizes a simulation study as a triple
of a sampling distribution, a family of performance functionals, and their Monte Carlo estimators
(@def-ademp, catalogue K.1). @sec-sim-bias treats bias and its Monte Carlo standard error, proving that
the Monte Carlo bias estimator is exactly unbiased for the true bias with a variance that shrinks as $1/R$
(@def-bias-mcse, K.2). @sec-sim-coverage develops the empirical and model-based standard errors and
interval coverage, proving the unbiasedness of the empirical variance and the binomial law of the coverage
estimator (@def-coverage, K.3). @sec-sim-mse proves the mean-squared-error decomposition into squared bias
plus variance, both as a population identity and as an exact finite-sample identity for the Monte Carlo
estimators (@thm-mse-decomposition, K.4). @sec-sim-misspec is the analytic heart of the chapter: it
derives the limiting coverage of a Wald interval as an explicit function of a single standardized
asymptotic bias parameter, showing that coverage is nominal exactly when the method is asymptotically
unbiased and that under a fixed specification bias coverage collapses to zero as $n\to\infty$, so that
*more data makes a biased method's intervals worse* (@thm-coverage-misspecification, K.5). @sec-sim-power
treats Type I error and power, which turn out to be the coverage theorem read through the duality of tests
and intervals (@def-power-type1, K.6). @sec-sim-efficiency anchors the variance comparisons of a
simulation in the Cramér-Rao bound (@thm-cramer-rao), the theoretical floor below which no regular method's
empirical standard error can fall. @sec-sim-robustness states, as precisely as an empirical finding can be
stated, the main robustness conclusion of the @phillippo2019thesis simulation study and its unanchored
extension (@prp-phillippo-robustness, K.7), tying each ranked claim either to a theorem proved earlier or
to the cited simulation evidence. @sec-sim-example carries a complete miniature simulation from its ADEMP
specification through every performance computation by hand. This chapter owns catalogue results K.1 to
K.7.

Throughout, $\theta$ denotes the scalar estimand (a relative effect $d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}$ on a stated
scale, in the applications of interest), $\hat\theta_n$ a method's estimator computed from a dataset of
size $n$, $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ the standard error that method reports for it, and $I_n$ the
associated nominal $(1-\alpha)$ interval. A simulation produces $R$ independent replicate values
$\hat\theta^{(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{(R)}_n$, with $\bar{\hat\theta}=R^{-1}\sum_{r}\hat\theta^{(r)}_n$
their average. We write $z_{\alpha/2}$ for the upper $\alpha/2$ standard-normal quantile, so that
$\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha/2$ and $P(|Z|\le z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$ for $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$; for the
usual $\alpha=0.05$, $z_{\alpha/2}=1.96$. The asymptotic toolkit is the one assembled in Chapter 5: the
weak law of large numbers, the central limit theorem, Slutsky's theorem (@thm-slutsky), the continuous
mapping theorem (@thm-continuous-mapping), and the delta method (@thm-delta-method).

The chapter uses a compact vocabulary of performance quantities. The following glossary collects them; the
single most important distinction, stressed throughout, is between the two kinds of standard error, the one
a *method* reports for a single analysis and the one the *simulation* reports for its own summary.

| Symbol | Name | Plain meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | per-replication sample size | patients in one simulated dataset |
| $R$ | replications | number of simulated datasets |
| $\theta$ | estimand | the known true effect we put into the world |
| $\hat\theta_n$ | estimate | one method's answer from one dataset |
| $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ | statistical (model-based) standard error | the uncertainty a method reports for *its own* estimate on one dataset |
| $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}$ | bias | average estimate minus the truth |
| $\mathrm{EmpSE}$ | empirical standard error | actual spread of the $R$ estimates, the truth about variability |
| $\mathrm{ModSE}$ | model-based standard error | average of the reported $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ across replications |
| $\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}$ | mean squared error | average squared distance of estimates from the truth |
| $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}$ | coverage | fraction of intervals that contain the truth |
| $\mathrm{MCSE}(\hat\mu)$ | Monte Carlo standard error | uncertainty in a *reported performance number* caused by using only $R$ replications |

The last row is not a property of any single analysis: it is the simulation's own sampling error, and it is
the quantity that shrinks when the analyst runs more replications. Confusing $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$, the
uncertainty in one estimate, with $\mathrm{MCSE}$, the uncertainty in the reported bias, coverage, or mean
squared error, is a frequent novice error; the two answer different questions and have different remedies.

## The ADEMP framework {#sec-sim-ademp}

A simulation study can be run badly in many ways: by simulating from a mechanism that no one can
reconstruct, by reporting an estimand the methods were never trying to estimate, by summarizing with a
statistic that hides the behavior of interest. @morris2019ademp distilled good practice into a five-part
specification whose initials spell ADEMP. We adopt it as the definitional backbone of the chapter and then
attach to it the probabilistic objects that the performance measures will be functionals of. The value of
the checklist is that each letter forces one decision into the open where it can be criticized: the aims
stop a study from being a fishing expedition, the data-generating mechanism makes the simulated world
reproducible, the estimand fixes what "the truth" even is before any method is judged against it, the
methods list what is being compared, and the performance measures decide what "good" means. A simulation
that skips any one of these can silently answer the wrong question.

::: {#def-ademp}
## The ADEMP framework for a simulation study
A **simulation study** is specified by five components.

1. **Aims (A).** The scientific questions to be answered, stated before any data are simulated: for
example, "quantify the bias of MAIC for the marginal $A$-versus-$B$ log-odds-ratio when a binary effect
modifier is omitted, as a function of its imbalance between trials."

2. **Data-generating mechanism (DGM, D).** A fully specified probability model $\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_n$
from which datasets of size $n$ are drawn: the covariate distribution, the treatment assignment, the
outcome model with all its parameters, and any features (overlap, effect-modification strength) that the
aims require to be varied across *scenarios*. A study comprises a finite set of DGMs, one per scenario.

3. **Estimands (E).** The target quantities, defined as functionals $\theta=\theta(\mathbb{P})$ of the
DGM. In the population-adjustment setting $\theta$ is a marginal relative effect $d_{ab(\mathcal{P})}$ in a
named target population $\mathcal{P}$ on a named scale $g$; because the DGM is known, $\theta$ is known
exactly, by analytic calculation or by a large auxiliary simulation.

4. **Methods (M).** The estimation procedures under comparison, each a measurable map from a dataset to a
triple $(\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)$ of a point estimate, a standard error, and a nominal
$(1-\alpha)$ interval. In this book the methods are the naive Bucher comparison (@thm-bucher-unbiased),
MAIC (Chapter 18), simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19), and multilevel network meta-regression
(Chapter 20), with their unanchored counterparts (Chapters 17, 26).

5. **Performance measures (P).** The summaries of a method's behavior across replications: bias, empirical
and model-based standard error, mean squared error, interval coverage, and, where the aim is testing,
Type I error and power. Each is a functional $\mu(F_n)$ of the sampling distribution $F_n$ of
$(\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)$ under the DGM at fixed $n$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The following table instantiates the five components for the running psoriasis comparison, so the abstract
checklist has a concrete referent before we turn it into probability.

| ADEMP component | The running psoriasis comparison |
|---|---|
| **Aims** | Quantify the bias and $95\%$ interval coverage of MAIC and of the naive Bucher comparison for the $A$-versus-$B$ PASI mean difference, as baseline-severity imbalance between the trials varies. |
| **Data-generating mechanism** | Draw $n$ patients per arm; baseline severity $x_1$ and age $x_2$ from chosen distributions with a set between-trial imbalance; PASI reduction from a linear model with an $x_1$-by-treatment interaction; independent outcome noise. The $BC$ trial is then reduced to arm means, mimicking the published aggregate data. |
| **Estimands** | $\theta=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$, the marginal $A$-versus-$B$ mean difference in the $BC$ population, computed exactly from the known model (@sec-sim-example). |
| **Methods** | MAIC (Chapter 18) and the naive Bucher comparison (@thm-bucher-unbiased), each returning an estimate $\hat\theta_n$, a standard error $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$, and a $95\%$ interval $I_n$. |
| **Performance measures** | Bias, empirical and model-based standard error, mean squared error, and coverage, each with its Monte Carlo standard error. |

Which pieces are which is worth stressing, because a novice designing a simulation must know what to fix and
what to vary. The covariate distributions and the outcome model are *chosen* by the analyst to resemble the
real trials; the between-trial imbalance and the effect-modification strength are *varied across scenarios*,
where each **scenario** is one cell of the design grid, that is, one combination of overlap, effect-modifier
imbalance, effect-modification strength, and sample size; the trial sizes are *set* to mimic the real
dossier; and the estimand is *derived* from the chosen model, not observed. Only the performance measures
are *outputs*. A method, stripped of the formal language of measurable maps, is in plain terms a computer
program that takes one simulated trial dataset and returns three things: a point estimate, a standard error,
and a confidence interval.

::: {.remark}
**How the truth is known, and how it is computed.** In a real analysis the target effect $\theta$ is
unknown, which is the entire difficulty; in a simulation the analyst *chose* the data-generating mechanism,
so $\theta=\theta(\mathbb{P})$ is determined and can be computed to any desired accuracy. Computing it is a
marginalization, not a guess. On the identity (mean-difference) scale of the running example, the marginal
estimand is the average of the conditional treatment effect over the target population's covariate
distribution,
$$
\theta=\int \tau(x)\,f_{\mathcal{P}}(x)\,dx,\qquad \tau(x)=\mu_1(x)-\mu_0(x),
$$
which for a linear outcome model reduces to evaluating the conditional effect at the covariate mean. On a
*non-collapsible* scale (@def-non-collapsibility), such as a marginal log-odds-ratio, one cannot average the
conditional log-odds-ratios: the truth must be obtained by *marginal standardization*, integrating the
conditional outcome probabilities over $f_{\mathcal{P}}(x)$ first, forming the marginal event probabilities
under each treatment, and only then taking the contrast. When the integral has no closed form (a survival
estimand, a probit-normal average), the analyst computes $\theta$ by a *large auxiliary simulation*, drawing
an enormous sample from the known mechanism and reading off the marginal effect; this auxiliary draw has
nothing to do with the $R$ replications and is made once, as accurately as compute allows. The lesson is
that even with the model fully known, "the truth" for a marginal, non-collapsible estimand is an integral,
which is exactly why population adjustment is subtle. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The fourth and fifth components hide the structure that makes the chapter mathematical. Fix a scenario
(a DGM) and a method. Applying the method to a dataset of size $n$ yields a random triple whose law,
written $F_n$, is the **sampling distribution**. Every performance measure is a deterministic functional of
$F_n$, hence a fixed number once $n$ is fixed; what the simulation reports is a Monte Carlo estimate of
that number.

::: {#def-sim-performance-functional}
## Performance measures as functionals; the two sample sizes
Let $F_n$ be the sampling distribution of $(\hat\theta_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,I_n)$ under a fixed DGM,
and let $\theta$ be the estimand. The **performance measures** are the functionals
$$
\mathrm{Bias}_n=\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]-\theta,\quad
\mathrm{Var}_n=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n),\quad
\mathrm{MSE}_n=\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2],\quad
\mathrm{Cov}_n=P(\theta\in I_n),
$$ {#eq-sim-functionals}
all expectations and probabilities taken under $F_n$. A **Monte Carlo experiment** draws
$R$ independent datasets from the DGM, producing independent and identically distributed (iid) replicate
triples $(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^{(r)}_n,I^{(r)}_n)$, $r=1,\dots,R$, each with law
$F_n$; the performance measures are estimated by their sample analogues over these $R$ replicates. Two
asymptotic regimes act on the experiment: the **statistical** limit $n\to\infty$, which governs the
functionals @eq-sim-functionals themselves and is the subject of the consistency theorems of earlier
chapters; and the **Monte Carlo** limit $R\to\infty$, which governs the precision with which the sample
analogues estimate @eq-sim-functionals. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Read $F_n$ as the joint distribution of everything one run of a method produces on a
dataset of size $n$: the estimate, the standard error it reports, and the interval it forms. It is a
distribution over a *triple*, not a single number, though most performance measures use only one margin of
it, such as the spread of $\hat\theta_n$. At a fixed $n$ this artificial world has a definite true bias and a
definite true coverage; we simply do not know them, because we cannot evaluate the distribution in closed
form. So we do the next best thing: we rebuild the artificial world $R$ times and average. Every performance
number in this chapter is such an average, and every one therefore comes with a Monte Carlo standard error
measuring how much the average would wobble if we reran the $R$ replications. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the two-sample-size view matters.** A consistency theorem controls $\mathrm{Bias}_n\to 0$ as
$n\to\infty$; it says nothing about how well $R$ replications *measure* $\mathrm{Bias}_n$ at a fixed,
practically relevant $n$. Conversely, no number of replications can reveal small-sample bias that the
chosen $n$ does not exhibit: pushing $R\to\infty$ at fixed $n$ converges the sample analogues to the exact
functionals @eq-sim-functionals at that $n$, not to their $n\to\infty$ limits. The analyst chooses the grid
of $n$ values to span the regime of interest and chooses $R$ large enough that Monte Carlo error does not
swamp the differences between methods. The performance measures below are designed so that each comes with
an MCSE quantifying exactly the second source of error. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The remaining sections instantiate the fifth ADEMP component, one performance measure at a time, proving in
each case (i) what functional of $F_n$ the measure targets, (ii) that the Monte Carlo estimator is unbiased
or consistent for it, and (iii) the size of its Monte Carlo standard error. This corresponds to K.1 in the
proof catalogue.

::: {.remark}
**Numbers to hang the symbols on.** It helps to carry one arithmetic instance through the definitions that
follow. In the running example the true effect is $\theta=1.5$ PASI points. Imagine five simulated trials of
the adjusted method returning estimates $0.9,0.9,1.4,1.9,1.9$ points. Their average is $1.4$, so the
estimated bias is $1.4-1.5=-0.1$ point; their spread gives an empirical standard error of $0.5$; and if three
of the five $95\%$ intervals contain $1.5$, the estimated coverage is $3/5=0.6$. Every definition below turns
one of these back-of-envelope numbers into a general formula, and @sec-sim-example works the same instance in
full, including why five replications are far too few to trust any of these numbers. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Bias and its Monte Carlo standard error {#sec-sim-bias}

Bias is the systematic component of an estimator's error: the gap between where its estimates cluster on
average and the truth. Its Monte Carlo estimator and the precision of that estimator are the content of
catalogue result K.2.

::: {#def-bias-mcse}
## Monte Carlo bias estimator, relative bias, and Monte Carlo standard error
With replicate estimates $\hat\theta^{(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{(R)}_n$ and known estimand $\theta$, the
**Monte Carlo bias estimator** is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}=\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\theta,
$$ {#eq-sim-bias}
and, when $\theta\neq 0$, the **relative bias** is $\widehat{\mathrm{RelBias}}=\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}/|\theta|$.
For any Monte Carlo performance estimator $\hat\mu$ targeting a functional $\mu$, its **Monte Carlo standard
error** is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution over the $R$ replications,
$\mathrm{MCSE}(\hat\mu)=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu)}$. In particular the Monte Carlo standard error of the
bias estimator is
$$
\mathrm{MCSE}(\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}})=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{R}},
$$ {#eq-sim-mcse-bias}
estimated in practice by $\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{R}$ with $\mathrm{EmpSE}$ the empirical standard error of
@def-coverage below. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The defining properties of the bias estimator are that it is exactly unbiased for the true bias at finite
$R$ and that its uncertainty is governed by @eq-sim-mcse-bias. We prove both. Unbiasedness matters because
it certifies that the number we headline as "the bias" is not itself systematically off: were the bias
estimator biased, our headline error would rest on a biased foundation that more replications could not
repair. What replications *do* shrink is the random wobble, at the $1/\sqrt{R}$ rate of @eq-sim-mcse-bias.

::: {#lem-sim-bias-unbiased}
## Exact unbiasedness and variance of the Monte Carlo bias estimator
Suppose $\mathrm{Var}_n=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n)<\infty$. Then for every $R\ge 1$ the Monte Carlo bias
estimator @eq-sim-bias satisfies
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\big]=\mathrm{Bias}_n,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\big)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{R},
$$ {#eq-sim-bias-moments}
so $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}$ is unbiased for the true bias $\mathrm{Bias}_n$, its standard deviation is the
Monte Carlo standard error @eq-sim-mcse-bias, and $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Bias}_n$ as
$R\to\infty$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The replicates $\hat\theta^{(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{(R)}_n$ are iid with mean
$\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]=\theta+\mathrm{Bias}_n$ and variance $\mathrm{Var}_n$. By linearity of
expectation,
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\big]
=\mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac1R\textstyle\sum_r\hat\theta^{(r)}_n\Big]-\theta
=\tfrac1R\sum_{r}\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta^{(r)}_n]-\theta
=\big(\theta+\mathrm{Bias}_n\big)-\theta=\mathrm{Bias}_n.
$$
Subtracting the constant $\theta$ does not change the variance, and the variance of an average of $R$ iid
terms each of variance $\mathrm{Var}_n$ is $\mathrm{Var}_n/R$ because cross-covariances vanish by
independence:
$$
\mathrm{Var}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\big)
=\mathrm{Var}\Big(\tfrac1R\textstyle\sum_r\hat\theta^{(r)}_n\Big)
=\frac{1}{R^2}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{R},
$$
which is the square of @eq-sim-mcse-bias. Finally, since $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}$ has mean
$\mathrm{Bias}_n$ and variance $\mathrm{Var}_n/R\to 0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Bias}_n$ as $R\to\infty$. $\square$
:::

The variance formula @eq-sim-bias-moments is what makes the $1/\sqrt{R}$ rate explicit and turns the choice
of $R$ into an arithmetic exercise.

::: {#cor-sim-replications-bias}
## Replications needed for a target bias precision
To estimate the bias with a Monte Carlo standard error no larger than a tolerance $m>0$ requires
$$
R\;\ge\;\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{m^{2}}.
$$ {#eq-sim-reps-bias}
Equivalently, halving the Monte Carlo standard error of the bias estimate requires quadrupling $R$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-sim-bias-unbiased the Monte Carlo standard error is $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n/R}$, which is
nonincreasing in $R$ and at most $m$ exactly when $\mathrm{Var}_n/R\le m^2$, that is when
$R\ge\mathrm{Var}_n/m^2$. Replacing $m$ by $m/2$ multiplies the right-hand side by $4$. $\square$
:::

To feel the $1/\sqrt{R}$ rate before trusting the algebra, fix a per-replication standard deviation
$\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}=\sigma$ and tabulate the bias Monte Carlo standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{R}$ and the
worst-case coverage Monte Carlo standard error $1/(2\sqrt{R})$ as $R$ grows.

| $R$ | bias MCSE $=\sigma/\sqrt{R}$ | coverage MCSE $\le 1/(2\sqrt{R})$ |
|---|---|---|
| $100$ | $0.100\,\sigma$ | $0.050$ |
| $1{,}000$ | $0.032\,\sigma$ | $0.016$ |
| $10{,}000$ | $0.010\,\sigma$ | $0.005$ |

Each tenfold increase in $R$ buys only a threefold ($\sqrt{10}$) reduction in Monte Carlo error, the
diminishing return that makes $R$ in the low thousands the usual compromise: enough to resolve differences
between methods, not so many that the study never finishes.

::: {.remark}
**Reporting discipline.** The bias and its Monte Carlo standard error must be reported together. A bias
estimate of $0.03$ with $\mathrm{MCSE}=0.05$ is consistent with no bias at all; the same estimate with
$\mathrm{MCSE}=0.003$ is firm evidence of a small systematic error. In the population-adjustment
literature, $R$ between $500$ and several thousand is typical; @morris2019ademp recommend choosing $R$ from
@eq-sim-reps-bias using a pilot estimate of $\mathrm{Var}_n$. Relative bias is often the more interpretable
summary when the estimand varies across scenarios, since a fixed absolute bias means something different
for an estimand of $0.1$ than for one of $3$. This Monte Carlo standard error is a property of the
*simulation*, measuring how firmly the study has pinned the bias down; it is a different object from the
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ a method reports for a single dataset, as the glossary at the start of the chapter
stresses. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This section corresponds to K.2 in the proof catalogue.

## Empirical and model-based standard error; coverage {#sec-sim-coverage}

Two notions of "the standard error" coexist in a simulation, and comparing them is the single most
informative diagnostic the study produces. The **empirical standard error** is the actual spread of the
estimates across replications, the truth about the estimator's variability. The **model-based standard
error** is what each method *claims* its variability to be, averaged across replications. When the claim
matches the truth, interval coverage is correct; when it does not, coverage fails, and the direction of the
failure is diagnostic. This is catalogue result K.3.

In plain terms, coverage answers a reliability question: if we could rerun the entire study many times, in
what fraction of runs would the reported $95\%$ interval actually contain the true effect? A trustworthy
method answers close to $95\%$. The two standard errors are the ingredients that determine that fraction, so
we define all three objects together.

::: {#def-coverage}
## Empirical standard error, model-based standard error, and coverage
With replicate estimates $\hat\theta^{(1)}_n,\dots,\hat\theta^{(R)}_n$, per-replicate reported standard
errors $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^{(1)}_n,\dots,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^{(R)}_n$, and nominal $(1-\alpha)$
intervals $I^{(r)}_n=[\hat L^{(r)},\hat U^{(r)}]$:

- the **empirical standard error** is the sample standard deviation of the estimates,
$$
\mathrm{EmpSE}=\sqrt{S^2},\qquad
S^2=\frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\big(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta}\big)^2;
$$ {#eq-sim-empse}

- the **model-based standard error** is the average of the reported standard errors,
$$
\mathrm{ModSE}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^{(r)}_n;
$$ {#eq-sim-modse}

- the **coverage** is the proportion of intervals that contain the estimand,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{1}\{\hat L^{(r)}\le\theta\le\hat U^{(r)}\}.
$$ {#eq-sim-coverage}
The target functionals are $\mathrm{Var}_n$ for $\mathrm{EmpSE}^2$, the average reported variance for
$\mathrm{ModSE}$, and the true coverage $\mathrm{Cov}_n=P(\theta\in I_n)$ for $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The empirical standard error squared is an honest estimate of the estimator's variance: the familiar
$(R-1)$ denominator makes it exactly unbiased.

::: {#lem-sim-empse-unbiased}
## Unbiasedness of the empirical variance and the Monte Carlo error of the empirical standard error
Suppose $\mathrm{Var}_n<\infty$. Then $S^2$ of @eq-sim-empse satisfies $\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\mathrm{Var}_n$, so
$S^2$ is unbiased for the sampling variance, and $S^2\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Var}_n$ as $R\to\infty$. The
empirical standard error $\mathrm{EmpSE}=\sqrt{S^2}$ is consistent for $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}$ but
slightly biased downward at finite $R$. If in addition $\hat\theta_n$ is normally distributed under the
DGM, then
$$
\mathrm{MCSE}(\mathrm{EmpSE})\;\approx\;\frac{\mathrm{EmpSE}}{\sqrt{2(R-1)}}.
$$ {#eq-sim-mcse-empse}
:::

::: {.proof}
The one idea behind the $(R-1)$ denominator is that each deviation is measured from the sample mean
$\bar{\hat\theta}$, itself computed from the same replicates and therefore sitting slightly closer to the
data than the unknown true mean $\nu$ does; the squared deviations come out systematically a touch too
small, and dividing by $R-1$ instead of $R$ corrects for the single degree of freedom spent estimating the
mean. The algebra makes this exact.

*Unbiasedness of $S^2$.* Write $\nu=\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]$ and expand each squared deviation about
$\nu$ rather than $\bar{\hat\theta}$. Using $\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})^2
=\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\nu)^2-R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2$ (the algebraic identity obtained by adding and
subtracting $\nu$ inside the square and noting the cross term sums to $-2R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2+\cdots$;
explicitly, $\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})^2=\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\nu)^2
-2(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\nu)+R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2$ and
$\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\nu)=R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)$, so the middle term is $-2R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2$
and the last two combine to $-R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2$), take expectations:
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})^2\Big]
=\sum_r\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\nu)^2]-R\,\mathbb{E}[(\bar{\hat\theta}-\nu)^2]
=R\,\mathrm{Var}_n-R\cdot\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{R}=(R-1)\mathrm{Var}_n,
$$
using $\mathrm{Var}(\bar{\hat\theta})=\mathrm{Var}_n/R$ from @lem-sim-bias-unbiased. Dividing by $R-1$ gives
$\mathbb{E}[S^2]=\mathrm{Var}_n$. Consistency $S^2\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Var}_n$ follows from the weak law of
large numbers applied to $\tfrac1R\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n)^2$ and to $\bar{\hat\theta}$ together with the
continuous mapping theorem (@thm-continuous-mapping), since
$S^2=\frac{R}{R-1}\big(\tfrac1R\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n)^2-\bar{\hat\theta}^2\big)$.

*Downward bias of $\mathrm{EmpSE}$.* The square root is strictly concave on $(0,\infty)$, so by Jensen's
inequality (@thm-jensen), $\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{S^2}]\le\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[S^2]}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}$, with
strict inequality unless $S^2$ is degenerate; hence $\mathrm{EmpSE}$ underestimates $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}$
on average, the bias vanishing as $R\to\infty$ because $S^2$ concentrates at $\mathrm{Var}_n$.

*Monte Carlo error under normality.* If the $\hat\theta^{(r)}_n$ are iid normal with variance
$\mathrm{Var}_n$, then $(R-1)S^2/\mathrm{Var}_n\sim\chi^2_{R-1}$, whose variance is $2(R-1)$; therefore
$\mathrm{Var}(S^2)=\big(\mathrm{Var}_n/(R-1)\big)^2\cdot 2(R-1)=2\,\mathrm{Var}_n^2/(R-1)$. Apply the delta
method (@thm-delta-method) to the smooth map $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$ at $x=\mathrm{Var}_n$, whose derivative is
$1/(2\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n})$:
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{EmpSE})=\mathrm{Var}(\sqrt{S^2})
\approx\Big(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}}\Big)^2\mathrm{Var}(S^2)
=\frac{1}{4\,\mathrm{Var}_n}\cdot\frac{2\,\mathrm{Var}_n^2}{R-1}=\frac{\mathrm{Var}_n}{2(R-1)}.
$$
Taking the square root and substituting the plug-in $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}\approx\mathrm{EmpSE}$ yields
@eq-sim-mcse-empse. $\square$
:::

One caveat deserves flagging next to the formula. The Monte Carlo standard error @eq-sim-mcse-empse is the
one performance-error formula in this chapter that *assumes normality* of $\hat\theta_n$: it comes from the
chi-square law of the sample variance and holds only approximately when the replicate estimates are skewed
or heavy-tailed. The bias, coverage, and mean-squared-error Monte Carlo standard errors carry no such
assumption.

Coverage is the proportion of a sequence of indicator variables, hence a binomial proportion, and its Monte
Carlo error is exactly the binomial standard error.

::: {#lem-sim-coverage-binomial}
## The coverage estimator is a binomial proportion
Let $C_r=\mathbf{1}\{\theta\in I^{(r)}_n\}$ and $\pi=\mathrm{Cov}_n=P(\theta\in I_n)$. Then
$C_1,\dots,C_R$ are iid $\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)$, the coverage estimator @eq-sim-coverage satisfies
$R\,\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(R,\pi)$, and
$$
\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}]=\pi,
\qquad
\mathrm{MCSE}(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}})=\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{R}}\;\le\;\frac{1}{2\sqrt{R}},
$$ {#eq-sim-mcse-coverage}
so $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}$ is unbiased and consistent for the true coverage $\pi$, with Monte Carlo
standard error estimated by $\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(1-\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}})/R}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Each replicate produces an interval $I^{(r)}_n$ with the law of $I_n$, so the event $\{\theta\in
I^{(r)}_n\}$ has probability $\pi$, and the events are independent across the independent replicates;
hence $C_r$ are iid $\mathrm{Ber}(\pi)$ and their sum is $\mathrm{Bin}(R,\pi)$. Then
$\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}]=\tfrac1R\sum_r\mathbb{E}[C_r]=\pi$, and by independence
$\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}})=\tfrac1{R^2}\sum_r\mathrm{Var}(C_r)=\tfrac1{R^2}\cdot R\,\pi(1-\pi)
=\pi(1-\pi)/R$, whose square root is @eq-sim-mcse-coverage. The bound $\pi(1-\pi)\le 1/4$ holds because
$\pi(1-\pi)$ is maximized at $\pi=1/2$, giving $\mathrm{MCSE}\le 1/(2\sqrt R)$. Consistency is the weak law
of large numbers for the iid bounded variables $C_r$. $\square$
:::

::: {#cor-sim-replications-coverage}
## Replications needed for a target coverage precision
To estimate coverage with Monte Carlo standard error at most $m$ for any true coverage requires at most
$R\ge 1/(4m^2)$ replications; near the nominal $\pi=0.95$ it suffices that $R\ge 0.95\cdot 0.05/m^2$. To
resolve coverage to within a Monte Carlo standard error of $m=0.0066$ at $\pi=0.95$ thus requires
$R\approx 1090$, the source of the common "use at least a thousand replications" recommendation.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @lem-sim-coverage-binomial the worst-case Monte Carlo standard error is $1/(2\sqrt R)$, at most $m$ when
$R\ge 1/(4m^2)$; substituting the specific $\pi=0.95$ into $\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)/R}\le m$ gives
$R\ge 0.95\cdot0.05/m^2=0.0475/m^2$, which for $m=0.0066$ is $0.0475/0.0066^2\approx 1090$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Replication planning as a workflow.** The two corollaries @cor-sim-replications-bias and
@cor-sim-replications-coverage are usually run as a four-step recipe, not as one-off formulas. (1) Run a
small *pilot*, perhaps $R_0=100$ replications of one representative scenario. (2) From the pilot, estimate
the ingredient the target needs: the estimator's variance $\mathrm{Var}_n$ (via $\mathrm{EmpSE}^2$) if bias
precision is the goal, or an anticipated coverage near $0.95$ if interval reliability is. (3) Choose a
tolerance $m$, the largest Monte Carlo standard error you are willing to report. (4) Solve for $R$:
$R\ge\mathrm{Var}_n/m^2$ for bias, $R\ge\pi(1-\pi)/m^2$ for coverage. The following table shows the coverage
Monte Carlo standard error near the nominal $\pi=0.95$ at the replication counts most studies actually use.

| $R$ | coverage MCSE at $\pi=0.95$, $\sqrt{0.95\cdot0.05/R}$ | resolves coverage to about |
|---|---|---|
| $500$ | $0.0097$ | $\pm 1.0$ percentage point |
| $1{,}000$ | $0.0069$ | $\pm 0.7$ percentage point |
| $2{,}000$ | $0.0049$ | $\pm 0.5$ percentage point |
| $5{,}000$ | $0.0031$ | $\pm 0.3$ percentage point |

The table explains the field's habits: $R=1000$ resolves coverage to well under a percentage point and bias
to about a thirtieth of the estimator's standard deviation, enough to separate a method covering at $0.88$
from one covering at $0.94$, while $R=5000$ is reserved for the finer comparisons among near-nominal methods.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The empirical-versus-model-based diagnostic.** Coverage of a Wald interval
$\hat\theta_n\pm z_{\alpha/2}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is governed by how the reported standard error
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$, summarized by $\mathrm{ModSE}$, compares with the true variability summarized by
$\mathrm{EmpSE}$. Three regimes occur. When $\mathrm{ModSE}\approx\mathrm{EmpSE}$ and the estimator is
approximately unbiased, coverage is near nominal: the intervals are the right width and centered correctly.
When $\mathrm{ModSE}<\mathrm{EmpSE}$, the method understates its own uncertainty, the intervals are too
narrow, and coverage falls below nominal; this is the dangerous failure, an overconfident method. When
$\mathrm{ModSE}>\mathrm{EmpSE}$, the intervals are wider than necessary and coverage exceeds nominal, an
inefficient but conservative failure. For MAIC and simulated treatment comparison the relevant
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is the sandwich standard error of @def-sandwich-variance and
@thm-maic-sandwich-variance (as a one-line refresher: the sandwich standard error corrects the naive one for
the fact that MAIC's weights are themselves estimated from the data rather than known in advance, and
ignoring that extra source of variability is what makes the reported standard error too small), and a naive
standard error that treats the estimated weights as fixed produces exactly the
$\mathrm{ModSE}<\mathrm{EmpSE}$ undercoverage that the sandwich correction repairs. For Bayesian
methods $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is the posterior standard deviation and $I_n$ a credible interval, whose
frequentist coverage the simulation measures. The next section shows that this diagnostic is only half the
story: coverage also depends on bias, and under bias coverage can fail no matter how accurate the standard
error. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This section corresponds to K.3 in the proof catalogue.

## The mean-squared-error decomposition {#sec-sim-mse}

Bias and variance are not competing summaries to be weighed by taste; they combine, exactly, into a single
measure of total error. The mean squared error is the expected squared distance from the estimand, and it
splits into a systematic part and a stochastic part with no remainder. This is catalogue result K.4 and the
one genuine theorem among the performance measures. It earns the name theorem, where the other performance
measures are definitions with elementary moment calculations, because it is an identity with content: it
certifies that total error splits cleanly into a part a simulation can blame on *noise* (variance,
shrinkable by a larger trial or a more efficient method) and a part it must blame on *the method itself*
(squared bias, removable only by fixing the model), with nothing left over. Every method's mean squared
error can therefore be attributed to exactly these two causes.

::: {#thm-mse-decomposition}
## Bias-variance decomposition of the mean squared error
For any estimator $\hat\theta_n$ of an estimand $\theta$ with $\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n^2]<\infty$,
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_n=\mathbb{E}\big[(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\big]=\mathrm{Bias}_n^{\,2}+\mathrm{Var}_n,
\qquad \mathrm{Bias}_n=\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]-\theta,\ \ \mathrm{Var}_n=\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n).
$$ {#eq-sim-mse}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\nu=\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]$ and insert it inside the square by adding and subtracting:
$$
(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2=\big((\hat\theta_n-\nu)+(\nu-\theta)\big)^2
=(\hat\theta_n-\nu)^2+2(\hat\theta_n-\nu)(\nu-\theta)+(\nu-\theta)^2.
$$
Take expectations term by term, using that $\nu-\theta=\mathrm{Bias}_n$ is a constant. The first term has
expectation $\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta_n-\nu)^2]=\mathrm{Var}_n$ by definition of the variance. The cross
term has expectation $2(\nu-\theta)\,\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n-\nu]=2(\nu-\theta)\cdot 0=0$, because
$\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n-\nu]=\nu-\nu=0$. The third term is the constant $(\nu-\theta)^2=\mathrm{Bias}_n^2$.
Summing,
$$
\mathrm{MSE}_n=\mathrm{Var}_n+0+\mathrm{Bias}_n^2,
$$
which is @eq-sim-mse. The finiteness $\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n^2]<\infty$ guarantees all three expectations
are finite. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters: four numbers, four questions.** The decomposition is the reason a simulation reports
bias, variance, mean squared error, and coverage as a set rather than picking one. Bias asks whether the
method is *valid*, that is, whether it aims at the right target; variance asks whether it is *precise*, that
is, how much its answers scatter; mean squared error @eq-sim-mse fuses the two into a single *accuracy*
score that lets a slightly biased but stable method beat an unbiased but volatile one; and coverage,
developed next, asks whether the method's *uncertainty statements* can be trusted. In an indirect comparison
these map directly onto the choice between MAIC, simulated treatment comparison, and multilevel network
meta-regression: the reweighting methods trade a little bias for controlled variance, the model-based
methods aim to reduce both, and only the full four-number report reveals which trade the data actually
reward. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The decomposition extends verbatim to vector estimands by summing over coordinates, which is the form
needed whenever a method is judged on several contrasts at once.

::: {#cor-sim-mse-trace}
## Vector form of the decomposition
For a vector estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n\in\mathbb{R}^k$ of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ with finite
second moments, the total mean squared error decomposes as
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n-\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2\big]
=\|\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n)\|_2^2+\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n),
$$ {#eq-sim-mse-trace}
where $\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n)=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n]-\boldsymbol{\theta}$
and $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}$ is the sum of the coordinatewise variances.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n-\boldsymbol{\theta}\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^{k}(\hat\theta_{n,j}-\theta_j)^2$
and apply @thm-mse-decomposition to each coordinate: the $j$-th term has expectation
$\mathrm{Bias}(\hat\theta_{n,j})^2+\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_{n,j})$. Summing over $j$, the squared biases
sum to $\|\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n)\|_2^2$ and the variances sum to the trace of the
covariance matrix, since the diagonal entries of $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_n)$ are exactly
the coordinate variances. $\square$
:::

The population identity @eq-sim-mse has an exact finite-sample shadow at the level of the Monte Carlo
estimators, with no approximation: the empirical mean squared error decomposes into the squared empirical
bias plus a multiple of the empirical variance.

::: {#lem-sim-mse-empirical-identity}
## Exact decomposition of the empirical mean squared error
Let $\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac1R\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\theta)^2$ be the Monte Carlo
mean-squared-error estimator. Then, identically in the data,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}=\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}^{\,2}+\frac{R-1}{R}\,\mathrm{EmpSE}^2,
$$ {#eq-sim-mse-empirical-identity}
with $\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}=\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta$ and $\mathrm{EmpSE}^2=S^2$ as above; and
$\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}]=\mathrm{MSE}_n$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Apply the same add-and-subtract step as in @thm-mse-decomposition, but to the *sample* mean
$\bar{\hat\theta}$ in place of the population mean. With $\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\theta
=(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})+(\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta)$,
$$
\sum_{r}(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\theta)^2
=\sum_{r}(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})^2
+2(\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta)\sum_{r}(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})
+R(\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta)^2.
$$
The middle sum vanishes because $\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})=0$ by definition of the sample
mean. Dividing by $R$ and using $\sum_r(\hat\theta^{(r)}_n-\bar{\hat\theta})^2=(R-1)S^2$ and
$\bar{\hat\theta}-\theta=\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}$ gives
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac{(R-1)S^2}{R}+\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}^{\,2},
$$
which is @eq-sim-mse-empirical-identity. For the expectation, take $\mathbb{E}$ of
@eq-sim-mse-empirical-identity: $\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}}^2]=\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}})
+(\mathbb{E}\widehat{\mathrm{Bias}})^2=\mathrm{Var}_n/R+\mathrm{Bias}_n^2$ by @lem-sim-bias-unbiased, and
$\mathbb{E}[\tfrac{R-1}{R}S^2]=\tfrac{R-1}{R}\mathrm{Var}_n$ by @lem-sim-empse-unbiased; their sum is
$\mathrm{Bias}_n^2+\mathrm{Var}_n=\mathrm{MSE}_n$ by @thm-mse-decomposition. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The bias-variance trade-off in population adjustment.** The decomposition @eq-sim-mse is the reason a
biased method can be preferred. Omitting a weakly imbalanced effect modifier from a MAIC introduces a small
$\mathrm{Bias}_n^2$ but, by retaining a larger effective sample size (@thm-maic-ess-bound), lowers
$\mathrm{Var}_n$; if the variance saving exceeds the squared bias incurred, the omission lowers the mean
squared error. The minimizer of @eq-sim-mse over the set of balanced moments is in general not the full
set, exactly the phenomenon that the no-extrapolation limit (@thm-maic-no-extrapolation) forces under poor
overlap, where balancing every moment drives the effective sample size, and with it the variance term,
toward catastrophe. A simulation study quantifies this trade-off scenario by scenario; the decomposition
guarantees that the two contributions it reports, squared bias and variance, account for the total error
with nothing left over. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This section corresponds to K.4 in the proof catalogue.

## Coverage under correct and incorrect specification {#sec-sim-misspec}

The coverage diagnostic of @sec-sim-coverage assumed an approximately unbiased estimator and asked whether
the standard error was right. The deeper question is what happens to coverage when the estimator is
*biased*, as it must be when a method's assumptions are violated: an omitted effect modifier, a misspecified
outcome model, a transportability assumption that does not hold. The answer, catalogue result K.5, is
sharp and at first counterintuitive: a fixed specification bias drives coverage not toward some degraded
constant but all the way to zero as the per-replication sample size grows. The intervals shrink around the
wrong value, and more data only sharpens the error.

::: {.remark}
**The phenomenon in plain words, before any formulas.** Here is the whole result in one breath. Suppose a
method is biased by a fixed amount: it aims at $1.0$ PASI points when the truth is $1.5$. As the trial grows,
the method's confidence interval shrinks, because more data makes each estimate more precise; but it shrinks
around the *wrong center*, $1.0$, not $1.5$. So the true value $1.5$ starts inside a wide early interval and
is squeezed out as the interval tightens: coverage *falls* as $n$ grows. This is counterintuitive because in
everyday statistics more data is always better; here more data makes a biased method's intervals *worse*,
since precision without accuracy is confident error. The worked example computes exactly this collapse for
the naive comparison in the running scenario, coverage dropping from $0.83$ to $0.48$ to $0.001$ as the
sample size climbs (@sec-sim-example). The rest of this section proves that the collapse is inevitable and
computes its exact rate; a reader content with the picture can skim the analysis and rejoin at
@cor-sim-fixed-bias-collapse. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We make this precise by computing the limiting coverage of a Wald interval as a function of a single
standardized bias. Throughout, $\theta$ is the true estimand and $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}$ is the value the
method's estimator actually converges to, the **estimand under the working model** (we write
$\theta_{\mathrm{work}}$, not $\theta_0$, to keep it distinct from the null value $\theta_0$ of the next
section). It equals $\theta$ when the method is correctly specified and differs from it otherwise; it is the
M-estimation target $\boldsymbol{\theta}^*$ of @def-m-estimator transported to the present scalar setting. A
concrete instance fixes the idea: when a MAIC omits an imbalanced effect modifier of strength $\beta_1$ whose
mean differs by $\Delta\bar x_1$ between the two trials, the omitted-covariate estimator no longer converges
to the target $\theta$ but to a shifted value $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}\approx\theta+\beta_1\,\Delta\bar x_1$;
the gap $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta$ is exactly the omitted-effect-modifier bias of @thm-failure-of-bucher
and @thm-aggregation-bias. Two further symbols appear below. The sequence $\sigma_n>0$ is the estimator's
*true* standard deviation at sample size $n$, a theoretical quantity the analyst never sees and which shrinks
to $0$ as $n$ grows; $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is the *operational* standard error the method reports and can
compute, and condition (C2) below says the two agree in the limit. The standardized bias
$b=\lim (\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n$ measures the fixed miss $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta$ in
units of the shrinking $\sigma_n$: if the miss is a fixed nonzero constant while $\sigma_n\to 0$, the ratio
blows up and we record $b=\pm\infty$, the case that will destroy coverage.

First, an elementary lemma about the function that will turn out to be the limiting coverage.

::: {#lem-sim-coverage-unimodal}
## The coverage curve
For fixed $z>0$ define $h:\mathbb{R}\to(0,1)$ by
$$
h(b)=\Phi(z-b)-\Phi(-z-b).
$$ {#eq-sim-coverage-curve}
Then $h$ is even, $h(0)=\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=2\Phi(z)-1$, $h$ is strictly increasing on $(-\infty,0)$ and
strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ with a unique global maximum at $b=0$, and $h(b)\to 0$ as
$|b|\to\infty$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Even.* Using $\Phi(-x)=1-\Phi(x)$, $h(-b)=\Phi(z+b)-\Phi(-z+b)=\big(1-\Phi(-z-b)\big)-\big(1-\Phi(z-b)\big)
=\Phi(z-b)-\Phi(-z-b)=h(b)$.

*Monotonicity.* Differentiate, using $\Phi'=\phi$ and the evenness of $\phi$:
$$
h'(b)=-\phi(z-b)+\phi(-z-b)=\phi(z+b)-\phi(z-b),
$$
since $\phi(-z-b)=\phi(z+b)$. For $b>0$ compare the arguments by absolute value: $(z+b)^2-(z-b)^2=4zb>0$,
so $|z+b|>|z-b|$, and because $\phi$ is strictly decreasing in the absolute value of its argument,
$\phi(z+b)<\phi(z-b)$, whence $h'(b)<0$ for all $b>0$. By evenness $h'(b)>0$ for $b<0$, and $h'(0)=0$.
Thus $h$ increases up to $b=0$ and decreases after, with a unique global maximum $h(0)=2\Phi(z)-1$.

*Limit.* As $b\to+\infty$ both $z-b\to-\infty$ and $-z-b\to-\infty$, so $\Phi(z-b)\to 0$ and
$\Phi(-z-b)\to 0$, giving $h(b)\to 0$; by evenness the same holds as $b\to-\infty$. $\square$
:::

A short table of the coverage curve $h(b)=\Phi(z-b)-\Phi(-z-b)$ at $z=1.96$ shows its shape at a glance: a
symmetric peak of $0.95$ at $b=0$, decaying on both sides, so that any nonzero standardized bias costs
coverage and a large one erases it.

| $b$ | $0$ | $\pm 0.5$ | $\pm 1$ | $\pm 2$ | $\pm 3$ | $\pm 5$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $h(b)$ | $0.950$ | $0.921$ | $0.830$ | $0.484$ | $0.149$ | $0.001$ |

**How to read the theorem below.** It computes the large-sample coverage of a Wald interval as this single
function $h(b)$ of the standardized bias $b$. The three conditions are the fine print that makes the
computation valid: (C1) the estimate is approximately normal around its own limit $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}$;
(C2) the reported standard error $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is asymptotically right for the true scale
$\sigma_n$; and (C3) the standardized bias settles to a value $b$, possibly $\pm\infty$. The payoff is the
dichotomy: coverage hits its nominal $1-\alpha$ exactly when $b=0$ (no bias), sits below nominal for any
finite $b\neq 0$, and collapses to $0$ when $b=\pm\infty$ (a fixed bias against a shrinking standard error).

::: {#thm-coverage-misspecification}
## Limiting coverage of a Wald interval under asymptotic bias
Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and let $z=z_{\alpha/2}$. For each $n$ let
$I_n=[\hat\theta_n-z\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n,\ \hat\theta_n+z\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n]$ with
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n>0$, and suppose there is a deterministic scale sequence $\sigma_n>0$ with
$\sigma_n\to 0$ such that:

(C1) *(asymptotic normality about the working-model target)*
$(\hat\theta_n-\theta_{\mathrm{work}})/\sigma_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$;

(C2) *(ratio-consistent standard error)* $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n/\sigma_n\xrightarrow{p}1$;

(C3) *(calibrated asymptotic bias)* $(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n\to b$ for some $b\in[-\infty,\infty]$.

Then the coverage of the true estimand $\theta$ satisfies
$$
\mathrm{Cov}_n=P(\theta\in I_n)\ \longrightarrow\
\begin{cases}
\Phi(z-b)-\Phi(-z-b), & b\in\mathbb{R},\\[2pt]
0, & b=\pm\infty.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-sim-coverage-limit}
Consequently, by @lem-sim-coverage-unimodal, the limiting coverage equals the nominal $1-\alpha=2\Phi(z)-1$
if and only if $b=0$, is strictly less than nominal for every finite $b\neq 0$, and degrades to $0$ as the
standardized bias diverges.
:::

::: {.proof}
The estimand lies in the interval exactly when the studentized statistic is within the critical values:
$$
\theta\in I_n
\iff |\hat\theta_n-\theta|\le z\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n
\iff -z\le T_n\le z,\qquad T_n:=\frac{\hat\theta_n-\theta}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}.
$$
Split $T_n$ at the working-model target $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}$:
$$
T_n=\underbrace{\frac{\hat\theta_n-\theta_{\mathrm{work}}}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}}_{W_n}
+\underbrace{\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}}_{D_n}.
$$
For the first term write $W_n=\dfrac{\hat\theta_n-\theta_{\mathrm{work}}}{\sigma_n}\cdot\dfrac{\sigma_n}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}$.
By (C1) the first factor converges in distribution to $Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and by (C2)
$\sigma_n/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\xrightarrow{p}1$; Slutsky's theorem (@thm-slutsky) gives
$W_n\xrightarrow{d}Z$.

*Finite $b$.* Write $D_n=\dfrac{\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta}{\sigma_n}\cdot\dfrac{\sigma_n}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}$.
The first factor is a deterministic sequence converging to $b$ by (C3) and the second converges in
probability to $1$ by (C2), so $D_n\xrightarrow{p}b$. Applying Slutsky's theorem again to
$T_n=W_n+D_n$ gives $T_n\xrightarrow{d}Z+b\sim\mathcal{N}(b,1)$. The points $\pm z$ are continuity points
of the limiting distribution function, so
$$
P(-z\le T_n\le z)\to P(-z\le Z+b\le z)=P(-z-b\le Z\le z-b)=\Phi(z-b)-\Phi(-z-b)=h(b),
$$
which is the first branch of @eq-sim-coverage-limit.

*Infinite $b$.* Suppose $b=+\infty$; the case $-\infty$ is symmetric. Fix $M>0$. Since
$D_n=(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ and $(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n\to+\infty$ while
$\sigma_n/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\xrightarrow{p}1$, we have $D_n\xrightarrow{p}+\infty$, so
$P(D_n<M)\to 0$. In words: we force the bias term $D_n$ to be at least a large constant $M$; the test
statistic $T_n$ is then dragged above $z$ unless the random part $W_n$ compensates by being very negative
(below $z-M$), an event of vanishing probability, so the interval almost never reaches up to $\theta$.
Formally, on the event $\{D_n\ge M\}$ we have $T_n\ge W_n+M$, hence $\{T_n\le z\}\subseteq
\{W_n\le z-M\}\cup\{D_n<M\}$, and therefore
$$
P(\theta\in I_n)\le P(T_n\le z)\le P(W_n\le z-M)+P(D_n<M).
$$
Letting $n\to\infty$, the first term tends to $\Phi(z-M)$ because $W_n\xrightarrow{d}Z$ and $z-M$ is a
continuity point, and the second tends to $0$; thus $\limsup_n P(\theta\in I_n)\le\Phi(z-M)$. As $M>0$ was
arbitrary and $\Phi(z-M)\to 0$ as $M\to\infty$, the limit is $0$, the second branch of
@eq-sim-coverage-limit.

The final consequences are @lem-sim-coverage-unimodal: $h(0)=2\Phi(z)-1=1-\alpha$ is the unique maximum,
so finite $b\neq 0$ gives $h(b)<1-\alpha$, and the infinite-$b$ branch gives $0$. $\square$
:::

The case that matters in practice is a *fixed* specification bias, where $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}\neq\theta$
does not depend on $n$ while $\sigma_n\to 0$; then $b=\pm\infty$ and coverage collapses.

::: {#cor-sim-fixed-bias-collapse}
## Fixed specification bias destroys coverage
Suppose (C1) and (C2) hold and the working-model target $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}$ is a fixed constant with
$\theta_{\mathrm{work}}\neq\theta$. Then $(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n\to\pm\infty$ as $\sigma_n\to 0$, so by
@thm-coverage-misspecification the coverage of $\theta$ tends to $0$: a consistently misspecified method
has asymptotic coverage zero, and its undercoverage *worsens* with increasing $n$.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta\neq 0$ a nonzero constant and $\sigma_n\downarrow 0$, the ratio
$(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n$ diverges to $+\infty$ if $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}>\theta$ and to $-\infty$ if
$\theta_{\mathrm{work}}<\theta$; either way $b=\pm\infty$ in (C3), and the second branch of @eq-sim-coverage-limit gives
limiting coverage $0$. Monotone worsening follows because the half-width $z\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\approx
z\sigma_n$ shrinks while the centering error $|\hat\theta_n-\theta|$ stays near the fixed
$|\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta|$, so the fixed miss eventually exceeds any shrinking half-width. $\square$
:::

::: {#cor-sim-correct-coverage}
## Correct specification yields nominal coverage
If the method is correctly specified, so that $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}=\theta$, and (C1) and (C2) hold, then $b=0$ and the
coverage of $\theta$ tends to the nominal level $1-\alpha$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Correct specification gives $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta=0$, hence $(\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta)/\sigma_n=0\to 0=b$, and the first
branch of @eq-sim-coverage-limit evaluates to $h(0)=\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=2\Phi(z)-1=1-\alpha$ by the definition
$\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha/2$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Two distinct ways coverage fails, and why bias is the worse one.** @cor-sim-correct-coverage shows
correct specification with an accurate standard error gives nominal coverage. The diagnostic of
@sec-sim-coverage concerns failures of (C2): if $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n$ is biased so that
$\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n/\sigma_n\xrightarrow{p}c\neq 1$, the studentized limit is $\mathcal{N}(0,1/c^2)$
and coverage tends to $2\Phi(cz)-1$, above nominal if $c>1$ and below if $c<1$; this is a fixed, often
modest, miscalibration. @thm-coverage-misspecification concerns failures of unbiasedness, failures of (C3)
with $b\neq 0$, and these are categorically worse: a *fixed* bias sends coverage to $0$. The practical
moral is that for a biased method, a larger trial or a longer Markov chain Monte Carlo run does not rescue
the interval; it tightens a confidently wrong statement. In the population-adjustment setting the fixed
bias $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}-\theta$ is precisely the aggregation or transitivity bias quantified earlier: the omitted
effect-modifier bias of @thm-failure-of-bucher and @thm-aggregation-bias, or the non-collapsibility-induced
scale mismatch of @def-non-collapsibility when contrasts are combined across populations on a
non-collapsible scale. A simulation study that reports coverage as a function of $n$ exhibits the collapse
of @cor-sim-fixed-bias-collapse directly: the telltale signature of a biased method is coverage that *falls*
as $n$ grows, distinguishing it from a merely inefficient one whose coverage stays near nominal.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The telltale signature.** Coverage that *falls* as $n$ grows is the fingerprint of bias; coverage that
*holds* near nominal as $n$ grows is the fingerprint of a merely inefficient method. A single simulation run
across a grid of sample sizes distinguishes the two at a glance, which is the practical reason coverage is
tabulated against $n$ rather than reported at one sample size. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This section corresponds to K.5 in the proof catalogue.

## Power and Type I error {#sec-sim-power}

When the aim of a study is detection rather than estimation, the relevant performance measures are the
Type I error rate and the power of a test. In the population-adjustment setting these are secondary, since
the goal is almost always a point estimate with an interval; but they are the natural language for
sample-size and design questions, and, as we show, they are governed by exactly the machinery of the
previous section through the duality between tests and intervals. This is catalogue result K.6.

::: {#def-power-type1}
## Wald test, Type I error rate, and power
For testing $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$ against $H_1:\theta\neq\theta_0$ at nominal level $\alpha$, the
**two-sided Wald test** rejects $H_0$ when $\theta_0$ falls outside the interval $I_n$, equivalently when
$$
|T_{0,n}|>z_{\alpha/2},\qquad T_{0,n}=\frac{\hat\theta_n-\theta_0}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}.
$$ {#eq-sim-wald-test}
The **Type I error rate** is the rejection probability when $H_0$ is true, $P_{\theta=\theta_0}(\text{reject})$,
whose target is the nominal level $\alpha$. The **power** at a true value $\theta_1\neq\theta_0$ is the
rejection probability $P_{\theta=\theta_1}(\text{reject})$. In a simulation each is estimated by the
proportion of replications in which $H_0$ is rejected, a binomial proportion whose Monte Carlo standard
error is given by @lem-sim-coverage-binomial with $\pi$ the true rejection probability.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The asymptotic level and power follow from one theorem, which is @thm-coverage-misspecification applied to
the null value, because the test rejects exactly when the interval misses $\theta_0$.

::: {.remark}
**How to read the power theorem, and why an ITC analyst should care.** The single input is the standardized
signal $\Delta_n=(\theta-\theta_0)/\sigma_n$: the true departure from the hypothesized null $\theta_0$,
measured in standard-error units, the mirror image of the standardized bias $b$ of the previous section.
Part (1) says a correctly centered test rejects a true null at the intended rate $\alpha$; part (2) gives
the power at a *local alternative*, meaning an alternative that shrinks toward the null as $n$ grows,
$\Delta_n\to\Delta$ finite, so that power settles at a value strictly between $\alpha$ and $1$ rather than
racing to $1$ (this shrinking is the device that keeps the calculation informative at every sample size);
part (3) says that against any fixed alternative the test eventually rejects with certainty. An
indirect-comparison analyst uses part (2) in reverse, as a sample-size rule: to detect a target effect with
prescribed power, solve @eq-sim-power for the $n$ that makes $\sigma_n$ small enough (@exr-sim-power carries
this out numerically). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-sim-power}
## Asymptotic level and power of the Wald test
Let $z=z_{\alpha/2}$ and suppose the estimator satisfies (C1) and (C2) of @thm-coverage-misspecification
with working-model target equal to the true value, $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}=\theta$, and define the
standardized signal $\Delta_n=(\theta-\theta_0)/\sigma_n$ measuring the departure from the hypothesized
$\theta_0$ in standard-error units.

1. *(Level.)* If $H_0$ is true, so $\theta=\theta_0$ and $\Delta_n\equiv 0$, then the Type I error rate
converges to $\alpha$:
$$
P_{\theta=\theta_0}(|T_{0,n}|>z_{\alpha/2})\to P(|Z|>z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha.
$$

2. *(Power, local alternatives.)* If $\Delta_n\to\Delta\in\mathbb{R}$, the power converges to
$$
1-\big(\Phi(z-\Delta)-\Phi(-z-\Delta)\big)
=\Phi(\Delta-z_{\alpha/2})+\Phi(-\Delta-z_{\alpha/2}).
$$ {#eq-sim-power}
For $\Delta>0$ the second term is negligible, giving the standard one-sided approximation
$\mathrm{Power}\approx\Phi\!\big(\Delta-z_{\alpha/2}\big)=\Phi\!\big(|\theta-\theta_0|/\sigma_n-z_{\alpha/2}\big)$.

3. *(Consistency, fixed alternatives.)* If $\theta\neq\theta_0$ is fixed and $\sigma_n\to 0$, so
$\Delta_n\to\pm\infty$, the power converges to $1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the same studentization as in @thm-coverage-misspecification, the test statistic decomposes as
$$
T_{0,n}=\frac{\hat\theta_n-\theta_0}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}
=\frac{\hat\theta_n-\theta}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}+\frac{\theta-\theta_0}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n}
=W_n+\Delta_n\cdot\frac{\sigma_n}{\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n},
$$
where $W_n\xrightarrow{d}Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ as shown there (using $\theta_{\mathrm{work}}=\theta$ in
(C1) and (C2)) and $\sigma_n/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\xrightarrow{p}1$.

*(1)* Under $H_0$, $\Delta_n\equiv 0$, so $T_{0,n}=W_n\xrightarrow{d}Z$; since $\pm z_{\alpha/2}$ are
continuity points, $P(|T_{0,n}|>z_{\alpha/2})\to P(|Z|>z_{\alpha/2})=2\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2})=2(\alpha/2)=\alpha$,
using $\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2})=1-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha/2$.

*(2)* If $\Delta_n\to\Delta$ finite, then $\Delta_n\cdot\sigma_n/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_n\xrightarrow{p}\Delta$
by Slutsky, and $T_{0,n}\xrightarrow{d}Z+\Delta\sim\mathcal{N}(\Delta,1)$. Hence the acceptance probability
$P(-z\le T_{0,n}\le z)\to\Phi(z-\Delta)-\Phi(-z-\Delta)=h(\Delta)$ as in @thm-coverage-misspecification,
and the power is $1-h(\Delta)$. Rewriting with $1-\Phi(z-\Delta)=\Phi(\Delta-z)$ and
$\Phi(-z-\Delta)=\Phi(-\Delta-z)$ gives @eq-sim-power. For $\Delta>0$ the term $\Phi(-\Delta-z)$ is the
upper tail beyond $\Delta+z>0$ and is small, leaving the one-sided approximation.

*(3)* If $\theta\neq\theta_0$ is fixed and $\sigma_n\to 0$, then $|\Delta_n|=|\theta-\theta_0|/\sigma_n\to\infty$,
so $h(\Delta_n)\to 0$ by the divergence branch of @lem-sim-coverage-unimodal (made rigorous by the same
bounding argument as in @thm-coverage-misspecification), and the power $1-h(\Delta_n)\to 1$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Tests are intervals turned inside out.** Part (1) is @cor-sim-correct-coverage read at the null: the
event $\{\theta_0\notin I_n\}$ has limiting probability $1-(1-\alpha)=\alpha$, which is the Type I error.
Part (2) is @thm-coverage-misspecification read with $\theta_0$ playing the role of the "true" value and
$\theta$ the role of the working-model target, so that the noncentrality $\Delta$ is the bias parameter
$b$ with a sign change. The power function @eq-sim-power evaluated at $\Delta=0$ returns
$2\Phi(-z_{\alpha/2})=\alpha$, recovering the level, as it must. This duality means a simulation that
reports interval coverage already contains the Type I error information; power requires only re-centering
the test at a hypothesized null. Population-adjustment simulations report power chiefly to inform the
sample size a future head-to-head or single-arm study would need, with $\Delta$ supplied by a target effect
size and $\sigma_n$ by the method's standard error at the planned $n$. For a concrete instance in the running
example: to detect a true $1.0$-point PASI advantage at $80\%$ power one needs
$\Delta=z_{0.025}+z_{0.20}=1.96+0.84=2.80$, hence a design reaching a sample size at which the method's
standard error has fallen to $\sigma_n=1.0/2.80=0.36$ points; the method's standard-error-versus-$n$ curve
then reads off the required $n$, and a less efficient method, needing the same $\sigma_n=0.36$ from a larger
$n$, is precisely the one a precision simulation flags. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This section corresponds to K.6 in the proof catalogue.

## The efficiency baseline {#sec-sim-efficiency}

A simulation that ranks methods by empirical standard error is estimating their relative efficiency, and
relative efficiency has a theoretical floor. The Cramér-Rao bound (@thm-cramer-rao) fixes the smallest
variance any regular estimator can achieve; the empirical standard error of the best possible method
approaches that floor, and the empirical standard error of any competitor measures its distance above it.
Anchoring the variance comparisons of a simulation to this baseline is what separates a finding that one
method is "more precise" from a finding that it is "near-optimal."

::: {.remark}
**What the baseline buys, in plain terms.** A precision ranking answers "is method X more precise than
method Y." The Cramér-Rao floor answers a more useful question: "is method X close to the best precision
*any* reasonable method could achieve, or is there room to do better?" Two pieces of fine print make the
statement rigorous, and a reader who wants only the conclusion may skip them. A *regular* model and estimator
(@def-regular-model, @def-efficient-estimator) are ones without pathological tricks: regularity excludes the
super-efficient estimators that beat the bound only at isolated parameter values by exploiting discontinuous
behavior, so the bound is a genuine floor for the methods a practitioner would use. *Uniform integrability*
of $\{n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\}_n$ is the technical condition that lets us pass from convergence of the
distribution to convergence of the variance; concretely it rules out heavy tails, the situation where a rare
enormous estimate, such as a single dominating MAIC weight under near-failing overlap, inflates the true
variance far above the nominal asymptotic value. The conclusion, stripped of fine print, is that the
empirical standard error estimates $\sqrt{V(\theta)/n}$, and $V(\theta)$ can never fall below the information
floor $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-sim-efficiency-baseline}
## Empirical standard error estimates the asymptotic variance, bounded below by the Cramér-Rao floor
Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an estimator of a scalar $\theta$ in a regular parametric model (@def-regular-model)
with per-observation Fisher information $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)>0$, and suppose
$\sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,V(\theta))$ with $\{n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\}_n$
uniformly integrable.

1. For each fixed $n$, the empirical variance $S^2$ from $R$ iid replications satisfies
$S^2\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Var}_n$ as $R\to\infty$, and $n\,\mathrm{Var}_n\to V(\theta)$ as $n\to\infty$;
hence $\mathrm{EmpSE}$ estimates $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_n}\approx\sqrt{V(\theta)/n}$.

2. If $\hat\theta_n$ is regular and asymptotically unbiased, then
$$
V(\theta)\ \ge\ \mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1},
$$ {#eq-sim-crlb-floor}
with equality if and only if $\hat\theta_n$ is asymptotically efficient (@def-efficient-estimator,
@cor-mle-efficient). Consequently the empirical standard error of any regular method satisfies, to first
order, $\mathrm{EmpSE}\gtrsim\sqrt{\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}/n}$, the **efficiency baseline**, and the
empirical relative efficiency $\mathrm{EmpSE}_2^2/\mathrm{EmpSE}_1^2$ of two methods estimates the ratio
$V_2(\theta)/V_1(\theta)$ of their asymptotic variances.
:::

::: {.proof}
*(1)* Sample-variance consistency is @lem-sim-empse-unbiased: $S^2\xrightarrow{p}\mathrm{Var}_n$ as
$R\to\infty$. For the second limit, convergence in distribution of $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n-\theta)$ to
$\mathcal{N}(0,V(\theta))$ together with uniform integrability of the squares
$\{n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2\}_n$ upgrades to convergence of second moments,
$n\,\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta_n-\theta)^2]\to V(\theta)$ (uniform integrability plus convergence in
distribution implies convergence of the corresponding expectations; see @billingsley1995). Asymptotic
unbiasedness, which the same uniform integrability gives via convergence of first moments
$\sqrt{n}\,\mathrm{Bias}_n\to 0$, yields $n\,\mathrm{Bias}_n^2\to 0$, so by @thm-mse-decomposition
$n\,\mathrm{Var}_n=n\,\mathrm{MSE}_n-n\,\mathrm{Bias}_n^2\to V(\theta)-0=V(\theta)$.

*(2)* The information for $n$ iid observations is $n\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)$ by additivity of Fisher
information over independent samples. For an exactly unbiased estimator the Cramér-Rao inequality
(@thm-cramer-rao) gives $\mathrm{Var}_n\ge (n\,\mathcal{I}_1(\theta))^{-1}$, hence
$n\,\mathrm{Var}_n\ge\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}$; letting $n\to\infty$ through part (1),
$V(\theta)\ge\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}$. The statement that no regular, asymptotically unbiased estimator
can have asymptotic variance below $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}$, with equality characterizing asymptotic
efficiency, is the local-asymptotic-minimax and convolution theory cited in Chapter 5 following
@def-efficient-estimator and realized by the maximum likelihood estimator in @cor-mle-efficient; we invoke
it here rather than reprove it. The relative-efficiency claim is then immediate: by part (1),
$\mathrm{EmpSE}_k^2\approx V_k(\theta)/n$ for method $k$, so the ratio estimates $V_2(\theta)/V_1(\theta)$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What a precision ranking means.** When a simulation reports that multilevel network meta-regression has a
smaller empirical standard error than MAIC under good overlap, @prp-sim-efficiency-baseline says it is
estimating a ratio $V_{\mathrm{ML\text{-}NMR}}/V_{\mathrm{MAIC}}<1$ of asymptotic variances, both bounded
below by the same Cramér-Rao floor $\mathcal{I}_1(\theta)^{-1}$. The reweighting methods pay for covariate
balance with the variance inflation factor $n/\mathrm{ESS}$ of @thm-maic-ess-bound and the variance-inflation
theorem of Chapter 18, lifting their $V(\theta)$ above the floor; a likelihood-based method that models the
outcome can sit closer to it. A simulation thus turns the abstract efficiency ordering into measured
numbers, with the bound certifying how much room for improvement remains. The uniform-integrability
hypothesis is not a formality: an estimator with occasional extreme values, such as MAIC under near-failing
overlap where a single weight dominates, can have a finite-sample variance far larger than its nominal
asymptotic variance, and the simulation will, correctly, report the large empirical standard error.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The empirical robustness finding {#sec-sim-robustness}

We now state the principal conclusion of the simulation literature on population adjustment, the synthesis
of the @phillippo2019thesis study and its successors. It is an **empirical** statement: it summarizes
measured bias and coverage across a designed grid of data-generating mechanisms, not a theorem with a
proof. We label it a proposition to record it precisely and to tie each of its claims either to a theorem
proved earlier in the book or to the cited simulation evidence, but its warrant is the simulation, and
different data-generating mechanisms could in principle reorder it. This is catalogue result K.7.

The following table summarizes the ordering at a glance; the proposition then states it precisely and ties
each row to a theorem. Here "good overlap" and "poor overlap" refer to whether the index and comparator
covariate distributions substantially share support. The literature has no single fixed cutoff, but it uses
the matching effective sample size relative to $n$ as the working diagnostic (@thm-maic-ess-bound, Chapter
18): overlap is comfortable when $\mathrm{ESS}$ remains a substantial fraction of the index sample size, and
worrying when it collapses to a small fraction, the regime of the no-extrapolation limit
@thm-maic-no-extrapolation. Below, EM abbreviates effect modifier.

| Method (anchored) | Key assumption | Bias | Variance | Coverage, good overlap | Coverage, poor overlap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ML-NMR, all EMs | correct EM model, adequate overlap | low | lowest | near nominal | degrades gracefully |
| STC, all EMs | correct outcome model | low | low | near nominal | can extrapolate |
| MAIC, all EMs | adequate overlap | low | higher ($n/\mathrm{ESS}$) | near nominal | low and unstable |
| MAIC, omitted EM | assumption violated | substantial | higher | below nominal, falls with $n$ | below nominal |
| Naive Bucher | transitivity (EM balance) | largest under imbalance | low | collapses with $n$ | collapses with $n$ |

::: {#prp-phillippo-robustness}
## Empirical robustness ordering of population-adjustment methods
Across data-generating mechanisms with correlated baseline covariates, varying covariate overlap between
the index and comparator populations, varying effect-modification strength, and varying inclusion or
omission of effect modifiers, the @phillippo2019thesis simulation study and its replications and extensions
